newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Nemtsov launches auction of foreign cars.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Nemtsov launches auction of foreign cars.

text.p: First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov on Friday launched the first auction of government-owned foreign limousines as part of a Buy-Russian campaign aimed at forcing officials to drive home-made cars.

Nemtsov, a charismatic liberal committed to cutting waste and reviving Russia's moribund economy, said the strategy would stimulate domestic car production and rake in much-needed cash to help pay the country's pensioners and state sector workers.
"It is absolutely incomprehensible that money from the state budget should go towards buying, for example, German vehicles," he told reporters at the Avtogarant complex on the outskirts of Moscow.

"Things will not change until our bureaucrats and deputies have felt with their own backsides all the delights of the Russian roads, until they have felt all the particularities of Russian cars," he joked.
But on Friday only seven government cars -- five Audis, one Saab and one Chevrolet Lumina -- were auctioned. Two failed to find a buyer and will have to be reauctioned at a later date.

Four of the cars sold went for around $20,000 against an average starting price of $60,000 and the fifth, a damaged Audi crashed by Aman Tuleyev, minister for Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) affairs, fetched just $10,000. The buyer said he was interested in the car parts.
But Nemtsov said he was satisfied with the outcome and teased journalists about scaring away potential buyers.

"Buying a car is an intimate business. Russians are not accustomed to buying a car in front of 300 journalists and lots of television cameras," he said, referring to the strong mass media interest the auction had spurred.

Making Russian officials drive Russian-made vehicles was one the first pledges made by Nemtsov after he quit his job as governor of the city of Nizhny Novgorod earlier this year to join President Boris Yeltsin's governing team.
Nizhny Novgorod is home to the GAZ car factory that produces the Volga sedans that Nemtsov intends ministers and other officials to drive from now on.
Yeltsin, who once said Nemtsov might one day succeed him as president, has thrown his weight behind the campaign to drop foreign cars from the government's limousine pool.
"Soon bureaucrats will only drive Russian cars," Yeltsin thundered in April when he kicked off the Buy-Russian drive.

Nemtsov, whose wide-ranging ministerial brief covers the energy sector, utilities, housing reform and the fight against corruption, said some 177 foreign cars would be sold off this year and slightly more than that in 1998.

He said sales of Russian-made cars had jumped by 13 percent in the first five months of 1997 compared with the same period last year and dismissed suggestions that domestic vehicles were more expensive than foreign makes.
Nemtsov, who has admitted he likes driving Mitsubishi's Pajero four-wheel drive vehicle, said the government's bid to replace its foreign limousines would help create new jobs for Russian workers.

The telegenic, curly-haired Nemtsov, who is one of Russia's most popular politicians, said in a book published this year entitled "The Provincial" that his main political objective was to improve life for ordinary Russian people.
Friday's auction drew a generally positive reaction.
"Nemtsov is a good guy. He is doing what he promised he would," said Misha, a driver.
Businessman Igor Karetsky, who was looking for a car for his wife, said he backed Nemtsov's campaign. "It's only right that taxpayers' money should be used to buy Russian cars," he said.
But not everyone shared their enthusiasm.
"I am a bit sorry to see the Audis go. They say that Volgas are better suited to our Russian roads but I don't agree," said Vladislav, one of the government's drivers. "I'd prefer to drive an Audi."
